what: The Construction Material Calculator estimates the bricks or blocks, cement, sand and crushed stone you need for three common jobs: building a wall, pouring a concrete slab or footing, and plastering a wall. It works in metric or imperial units.
Brick sizes from several countries, standard concrete mixes and the usual dry-volume factors are built in, and you can edit all of them. The working is shown step by step so you can check it.
uses: Know roughly what to buy before asking for quotes.
Count the bricks or blocks for a garden or boundary wall.
Find the concrete volume and cement bags for a slab.
Estimate cement and sand to plaster rooms.
Compare a builder's material list with your own estimate.
tutorial: Pick metric or imperial, then a brick wall, a concrete slab or plaster.
For a wall: length, height, doors and windows to subtract, and thickness. For concrete: length, width, thickness and how many. For plaster: wall size, sides and thickness.
Choose a brick size and mortar mix, or a concrete mix such as 1 : 1.5 : 3. Every number can be edited.
Add wastage (5–10% is usual) and set your cement bag size.
Open the advanced box to change the dry volume factor or material densities.
See bricks, cement bags, sand, stone and water, and how each was worked out. Copy the results for your supplier.
features: Switching converts the numbers you typed.
UK/Europe, US modular, Australia, India modular, South Asia traditional and concrete block.
Volume plus approximate weight for ordering.
Each step is listed below the result.

example.title: Worked example: a 10 m garden wall
example.text: A single-brick wall 10 m long and 3 m high with UK bricks (215 × 102.5 × 65 mm) and 10 mm joints covers 30 m². Each brick with its joint covers 0.225 × 0.075 m, so about 1,778 bricks, or 1,867 with 5% wastage. The mortar at 1:5 needs about 3.5 bags of 50 kg cement (so buy 4) and about 0.6 m³ of sand.

tips: Order a little extra; running out mid-job costs more than leftovers.
Ready-mix concrete is sold by volume, so use the concrete volume figure.
Measure openings (doors, windows) so you don't overbuy.
Ask your supplier for the real density and bag size of their materials.
problems: Doors and windows are bigger than the wall
Check you typed the openings in square meters or square feet, not lengths.
Numbers changed when I switched units
That is on purpose: your sizes are converted. Retype them if you prefer round numbers.
Builders use local rules of thumb and different wastage. Compare the steps and adjust the factors.
